scenario: AITA for refusing an additional guest at our wedding | Thanks for watching this post. First time writing here and non-native English speaker. I am getting married very soon. As you can imagine, this takes a lot of preparation. I'm talking here about the civil wedding, which will be very intimate and consequently restricted to our very close family: parents, siblings and, in my case, godparents and their children. The wedding will happen in another country, so this takes a lot of preparation as it is in another culture. When I made the invitations, I've been clear: I invited my parents (2 p.) and my godparents' family (4 p.). I've been very flexible, I told everyone that they could join us anytime they like (i.e., arrive in the country when they wish because I understand it's complicated when you have 4 different jobs etc) as long as they'll be present for the ceremony. Moreover, because the destination is far, my in-laws kindly proposed to offer the accommodation to all of them. The wedding is now in one month and I just received a message from my godmother saying that they have booked the flights, and they will be 5 because the gf of my cousin is joining. That's where I am really feeling uncomfortable: I receive this as a 'fait accompli' (done deal) without any prior consultation, without even asking me if that's ok to have an additional person (that I've never met). I've always been clear about the number of people invited. I just can't stand to receive this kind of 'news' via a late evening text message. It's not that I'm against that additional person. It's just the way that I'm put in front of this, as if I had nothing to say. And we're not talking about the 'party' wedding, but something very special that is meant to be in strict intimacy. Moreover, I know that they have their tickets since 1 month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip etc. So they literally waited 1 month to announce it, now that the date is getting closer. I just don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything, and to ask if it's possible, etc. In sum, they just invited someone at my wedding, someone that wasn't ever planned and that I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying: 'I'm confused by your news, I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e. you) for our wedding. Why haven't you called me and asked me before booking anything? I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it, as it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. The solution to this situation, I am afraid, does not lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise.' So: Am I the asshole? More precisely: Am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Thanks.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being an asshole in this situation. Let me start by understanding what's going on here. I'm getting married soon, and it's a civil wedding that's supposed to be very intimate. That means only our very close family is invited: parents, siblings, godparents, and their children. Since the wedding is in another country, it's a lot of work to organize everything, especially because it's in a different culture. When I sent out the invitations, I was clear about the number of people I was inviting. I told everyone they could come anytime they wanted, as long as they were present for the ceremony. I was flexible because I understand that coordinating with four different jobs can be complicated. Plus, my in-laws offered to provide accommodation for everyone, which was really kind. Now, just one month before the wedding, I received a message from my godmother saying that they've booked their flights and that there will be five people coming instead of four. The fifth person is the godfather of my cousin, someone I've never met. I'm really uncomfortable with this because it feels like a done deal without any prior consultation. They didn't even ask me if it's okay to have an additional person. I've always been clear about the number of guests, and I can't stand receiving this kind of news via a late-night text message. It's not that I'm against having this additional person. It's just the way I'm being put in front of this decision, as if I had nothing to say. We're not talking about a big party wedding but something very special meant to be strictly intimate. Plus, I know they've had their tickets for a month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip, etc. They literally waited a month to announce this, now that the date is getting closer. I don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything and to ask if it's possible. In summary, they just invited someone to my wedding, someone who was never planned and whom I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying I'm confused by their news. I explained that I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e., them). I asked why they didn't call me and ask before booking anything. I said I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it because it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. I mentioned that the solution to this situation doesn't lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise. So, am I the asshole? More precisely, am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Alright, now that I've laid out the situation, I need to think about whether my actions are justified or if I'm overreacting. Let's break it down step by step. First, I was clear about the number of guests from the beginning. I specified who was invited, and I was flexible about the timing of their arrival. That shows that I was considerate of their needs and tried to make things as easy as possible for them. Then, they waited a month to inform me that they're bringing an additional person. This is problematic because it changes the plan significantly. They didn't consult me beforehand, which is disrespectful. It's one thing to have a few extra people, but it's another to change the guest list without the host's approval, especially when the event is supposed to be intimate. I sent a polite message expressing my confusion and discomfort. I asked why they didn't communicate with me before making such a decision. I made it clear that I'm opposed to this change because it goes against what we've been planning. I also mentioned that the solution isn't within my hands, implying that I'm not the one who can make this change. Now, the question is: Am I being an asshole for refusing this and for writing to them clearly about my stance? To determine this, I need to consider the following points: 1. **Communication**: Did they communicate properly with me before making the decision? It seems they didn't. They waited until the last month to inform me, which is not ideal. 2. **Respect for Boundaries**: I set clear boundaries about the number of guests. They ignored that, which could be seen as not respecting my wishes. 3. **Impact on the Event**: Adding an extra person changes the dynamics of the event, especially since it's supposed to be intimate. This could make the event less special for me. 4. **My Reaction**: I expressed my concerns politely but firmly. I didn't yell or insult them; I just stated my position clearly. 5. **Alternative Solutions**: Did I offer any alternative solutions, or did I just refuse the change? It seems I didn't offer any alternatives, which could be seen as being inflexible. 6. **Their Perspective**: Maybe they thought it was a small change and didn't realize how it would affect me. They might have felt it was okay to add someone without asking. 7. **Cultural Differences**: Since the wedding is in another country, there might be cultural differences in how such decisions are made. Perhaps in their culture, it's more common to make such decisions without consulting the host. 8. **My Feelings**: It's important to acknowledge my feelings of being disrespected and having my plans disrupted. These feelings are valid, and it's okay to stand up for myself. 9. **Potential Compromise**: Is there a middle ground? Maybe they could have communicated earlier, or I could have been more open to the change if it was discussed beforehand. 10. **Long-term Relationship**: How does this situation affect my relationship with my godparents and in-laws? It's important to maintain harmony, especially since they're providing accommodation. Considering all these points, I need to evaluate whether my reaction is justified or if I'm being too rigid. On one hand, I was clear about the guest list, and they didn't respect that. They made a significant change without consulting me, which could be seen as disrespectful. My reaction was to express my discomfort and firmly state my position, which is reasonable. On the other hand, I didn't offer any alternative solutions or show willingness to compromise. I just refused the change outright, which could be seen as being inflexible. Additionally, they might have had their reasons for waiting to inform me, even if it wasn't ideal. Moreover, since the wedding is in another country, there might be cultural differences in how such decisions are made. They might not have realized how important it was for me to have a strictly intimate event. In conclusion, while my feelings are valid, and their lack of communication is problematic, my refusal without offering any alternatives could be seen as being inflexible. It might be better to have an open conversation about the issue, express my concerns, and see if a compromise can be reached. However, if I feel strongly that the additional guest would ruin the intimacy of the event, then standing my ground might be necessary. It's a delicate balance between maintaining harmony and staying true to my wishes for the wedding. In the end, whether I'm being an asshole depends on how I approach the situation moving forward. If I can communicate my feelings respectfully and be open to dialogue, then I'm not being an asshole. If I stubbornly refuse to consider any alternatives, then it might come across as being inflexible or unkind.
